Hooks that kick off async work (API calls, debounced fetches, awaited sends) must capture an identity/version token when the operation starts and re-validate it before applying the result to state. Without this guard, a slow response can land after the surrounding context (session, thread, pane, turn) has moved on, overwriting newer state, resurrecting stale data, or duplicating/misplacing entries.

Practical rules:
- Snapshot the relevant state (ids, revision, attached files, draft text) at the moment the async call is issued, not when it resolves.
- Use a monotonically increasing request counter or a bound/ownership ref (e.g. `const request = ++requestRef.current`) and check it still matches `requestRef.current` (or `boundRef.current`) before committing the result.
- When deriving a "refresh" or "cache" key that gates whether a fetch is current, make sure it changes on every state transition that should invalidate old results (e.g. include message counts, not just a status flag), otherwise a new turn/session can be mistaken for still-current data.
- When merging async/canonical data with optimistic/local data (e.g. reconciling saved history with live-only messages), match by stable id and insertion position instead of positional/backward scans, and skip entries that don't belong to the content being merged to avoid duplicates.
- When a component instance can be retired (unmounted, remounted for a different thread/session) while an async call is in flight, don't let its continuation decide based on its own stale ref/state — validate against the current owner (current thread id, draft revision, or lifetime) before writing back.

Example pattern:
```ts
const requestRef = useRef(0);

useEffect(() => {
  const request = ++requestRef.current;
  fetchData(params).then((result) => {
    if (request === requestRef.current) {
      setResult(result); // only apply if still the latest request
    }
  });
}, [params]);
```

Applying this consistently prevents races where late-arriving async results corrupt UI state, duplicate messages, or silently drop newer user input.
